native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Increasing government education expenditure is associated with smaller per-capita-income gains in Sub-Saharan Africa than in the broader lower-middle-income aggregate it is largely nested in, and in neither aggregate is the long-run association positive. In trend-adjusted levels the association is negative (LMC: -0.20 ln points per +1pp of GNI, p=0.002; detrended r=-0.55), but the sign reverses in year-to-year changes (LMC: +0.022, p=0.035; +0.040 with trend, p<0.001, i.e. ~+2 to +4% growth per +1pp), a fragility that disappears when the sample is shortened to 1991-2015 (-0.031, p=0.48) and is largely absorbed by enrolment controls. Sub-Saharan Africa sustained the highest expenditure shares in the panel (4.30% vs 3.50% of GNI; peak 6.10% in 1997 vs 3.87%), yet its income exists only for 2011-2015 (n=5), so its implied slope (-0.10; SSA interaction +0.35, p=0.24, N=46) is descriptive rather than estimated, and the SSA/LMC overlap attenuates any true difference toward zero. In the only comparable window (2011-2015) SSA spent more (3.41% vs 3.16%) and grew far less (+5.1% vs +13.8%), with a negative year-to-year co-movement (r=-0.47), and its 2015 income level equalled the lower-middle-income aggregate's 2009 level while the gap widened from 171 to 331 US$. The mechanism is access rather than income: SSA primary gross enrolment rose 60.6 to 97.0 and secondary 14.8 to 43.4 (still ~21pp below LMC) with no detectable enrolment payoff to spending changes (secondary -0.26, p=0.21; primary +0.25, p=0.59), whereas LMC shows a negative enrolment response (-0.79, p=0.007). Associations only: two group aggregates with 5 SSA income observations cannot support causal claims.
native_result.WorkflowB: WDI wide export (12x45) reshaped to long (group x series x year); QC of non-numeric/blank cells (0 non-numeric, 128/492 blank, no imputation). Step A: decade trends of education expenditure, enrolment, exports, LFPR and income levels; levels-vs-changes correlations and detrended correlation. Step B: within-LMC OLS with Newey-West (4 lags) in trend-adjusted levels (contemporaneous, lag 1/2/3; lag 2 primary) and in first differences, reporting Durbin-Watson and residual AR(1). Step C1: pooled group-intercept model with SSA x education interaction (N=46) reported only as a low-power reference; C2: common 2011-2015 window comparison (n=5 per group). Step C3/E2: mechanism models of gross enrolment on education expenditure in levels and differences for both groups with SSA interactions. Step D: secondary specification with enrolment, export growth and labour-force controls restricted to 1991-2015. Limitations documented: 5 SSA income observations, 1991-2015 control window, SSA-as-subset-of-LMC attenuation, GNI per capita instead of GDP per capita and adjusted-savings measure instead of % of government expenditure (metadata discrepancy with datasets.json), endogeneity/denominator effects, and the infeasibility of PCSE or cluster-robust standard errors with two aggregate panels.
